messages.subject: SE's or CI's around Nhats in oSCR
messages.subject_clean: SE's or CI's around Nhats in oSCR
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks,

How does one go about correctly getting bounds on Nhat in oSCR? In the oSCR.fit(), does the warning:

 Nhat(state-space) = exp(d0.)*nrow(ssDF)
  (caution is warranted when model contains density covariates)

just mean that

Nhat<- exp(modelOutput$outStats[3,"mle"])*nrow(ssDF[[1]])

is insufficient and must include the density covariates, so that getting bounds on Nhat instead requires:

#lower bound on Nhat, which includes - Std. errors of intercept and covariates
Nhat_loCI <- exp(modelOutput$outStats[3,"mle"] - 1.96*modelOutput$outStats [3,"std.err"] + modelOutput$outStats[4,"mle"] - 1.96*modelOutput$outStats[4,"std.err"]) * nrow(ssDF[[1]])

#upper bound on Nhat, which includes + Std. errors of intercept and covariates
Nhat_hiCI <- exp(modelOutput$outStats[3,"mle"] - 1.96*modelOutput$outStats [3,"std.err"] + modelOutput$outStats[4,"mle"] - 1.96*modelOutput$outStats[4,"std.err"]) * nrow(ssDF[[1]])

Or is that wrong and am I missing something?

I know, I think!, that (1) predict.oSCR() provides point estimates of Nhat, which is the sum of E(N) across all state-space pixels; that (2) in a Bayesian approach, bounds are created by looking at the distribution of summed z's across MCMC iterations; and that bounds around this realized density/abundance estimate are *not* the same as the bounds around the expected densities, which are obtained with get.real().

Apologies if I'm being obtuse,
Thanks,
Cat

messages.body_plain:
hi Cat,
 I'm actually not clear from your post here whether you have covariates on density in the model or not.
 To better understand what's going on can you show the printed summary of your model?

 If there are covariates on density then there's not an easy way to do this.  You can actually, in principle, rig-up the delta approximation to Var( \sum  \hat{D}(s) )     but that's the expected abundance and not the realized abundance and I think in practice  one would always want the realized abundance and it's CI.  But there is not an easy way to do this.  At one time we talked about using a bootstrap procedure to do this and I still think that's the way to go.  I think for the next oSCR workshop we'll have that worked out maybe ;)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Cat,

Just echoing what Andy says. This is a high priority feature that shouldn’t be too hard to implement, but I just haven’t had the time to sit down and code it up. There is an interesting discussion on a few ways to do this in the following paper:

Estimating population size by spatially explicit capture–recapture

Murray G. Efford,Rachel M. Fewster,

https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1600-0706.2012.20440.x

A perhaps convenient result in this paper is that “The estimated number in the area bounded by the outermost traps differed little between a homogeneous density model and models with a quadratic trend in density or a habitat effect on density, despite evidence that the latter models fitted better.”.

The next workshop is potentially in the summer, so the hour glass has been tipped I guess 😊

If you, or anyone else, has had any success with this, we’d be happy to hear about it!

Chris

I think the bootstrap idea came up in the context of subsets of the statespace maybe.

scr0 <- oSCR.fit(model = list(D~session, p0~maxtemp, sig~1),
                 DorN="D",
                 encmod="CLOG",
                 trimS=data$scrFrame$mdm,
                 scrFrame=data$scrFrame,
                 ssDF=list(ss[[1]],

                           ss[[3]],
                           ss[[4]],
                           ss[[5]],
                           ss[[6]],
                           ss[[7]],
                           ss[[8]],
                           ss[[9]]),
                 rsfDF=list(rsfDF[[1]],
                            rsfDF[[2]],
                            rsfDF[[3]],
                            rsfDF[[4]],
                            rsfDF[[5]],
                            rsfDF[[6]],
                            rsfDF[[7]],
                            rsfDF[[8]],
                            rsfDF[[9]]),
                 RSF=TRUE,
                 telemetry="ind")

Thank you for any help you might offer!!

messages.subject: Re: [oscr] Trap covariates + rsfDF covariates?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joël, does this covariate vary by trap or just occasion?  If the former, you'd need to have unique values for all pixels in your rsfDF to reflect the spatial variation.  I assume it's more likely that temperature varied over time the same for every trap, in which case you could simply put a single value in the rsfDF that corresponds to the mean (x = 0, if standardized).  Technically it shouldn't matter what that value is so long as it's the same for every pixel.  This way, the model is acknowledging variation by occasion for all traps that is constant across space and, thus, should not interfere with the RSF.  Let me know if that works!

messages.subject: Reduce model run-time?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am wondering how I can speed up model computation time.

The data I have consist of:

-9 sessions

-800-1200 traps in each session

-~300-500 captures per session

-16-18 occasions in each session

-3 weather covariates

-1 spatial covariate that divides
the study area into 3 zones

-1 individual covariate (sex

-An RSFdf with 11 habitat
variables

I have run the following models for only 2 sessions:

Model without RSF and with temperature-dependent
detection:

Mod1 <- oSCR.fit(scrFrame=data$scrFrame,

                 ssDF=list(ss[[1]],

                                   ss[[2]]),

                 trimS=data$scrFrame$mdm,

                 model =
list(D~session,p0~maxtemp,sigma~1,path~1))

Model with
RSF and temperature-dependent detection:

Mod2 <-
oSCR.fit(scrFrame=data$scrFrame,

                 ssDF=list(ss[[1]],

                                  ss[[2]]),

                 rsfDF=list(rsfDF[[1]],

                                   rsfDF[[2]]),

                 RSF=TRUE,

                 telemetry="dep",

                 trimS=data$scrFrame$mdm,

                 model = list(D~session,p0~maxtemp+maxtemp2,sigma~1,path~1))

Model with
RSF, temperature-dependent detection, and area-dependent density:

Mod3 <-
oSCR.fit(scrFrame=data$scrFrame,

                 ssDF=list(ss[[1]],

                                  ss[[2]]),

                 rsfDF=list(rsfDF[[1]],

                                   rsfDF[[2]]),

                 RSF=TRUE,

                 telemetry="dep",

                 trimS=data$scrFrame$mdm,

                 model = list(D~session + area,p0~maxtemp+maxtemp2,sigma~1,path~1))

Mod1 took 196
minutes to run, Mod2 took 300 minutes to run, and Mod3 took 762 minutes to run.
I am wondering if there is any way to shorten the computation time of the
models? My data are in UTMs which I have divided by 1000, and my state space
resolution is 0.1km (100m). Here is a plot of my state space.

As I am working
with snakes with small movement ranges, I cannot reduce the resolution further and,
in fact, I would like to increase the resolution if possible. I would also like
the models to include all sessions. However, the current model run-times make
this impossible. To speed things up, I am also using the AWS EC2 server.

I am really hoping I
have simply skipped a step that could make this faster. Any insights would be
greatly appreciated.

Thank you in
advance,

Joel

messages.subject: Re: [oscr] Reduce model run-time?
messages.body_plain:
hi Joel,
 This is an interesting study you have. I have good news and bad news for you. First, the good news is that these models ran at all, you must have a fast computer!  The other good news is that 700 minutes or so really isn't too bad. I mean if you have a bunch of cores and you don't mind waiting overnight or whatever, you can run a bunch of models in a day or two.
The bad news is I think you need to increase your trimS a bit, I don't think mdm is sufficient in general. So that's going to cost you.

 There isn't much else you can do in oSCR -- using a coarser state-space and the trimS option are the main things you can do.  One other option which I've tried in some cases is combining traps. If traps are very very close together you can merge them and combine the encounters.  Maybe that doesn't make sense in your case, but just an idea...

 If run time really deteriorates if you increase SS resolution or trimS then you might consider the SECR package. This is more efficient computationally (oSCR is written in pure R which really slows things down.  I think we could get some big improvements with careful thinking and coding but that's a big project and without specific funding to motivate it, or a grad student, it's probably not going to happen until I retire.

regards
andy

messages.subject: Re: [oscr] Reduce model run-time?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Joel, can you share some output? Curious what the model results look like.

I disagree with Andy about the trimS, and clarifying that you appear to be using mdm (maximum distance moved) and not mmdm (mean maximum distance moved). The former is a sampling extreme (i.e., the farthest you know an individual has moved), while the latter is a population average that can certainly miss the required local evaluation space for individuals with large movements. In either case, you need to be careful when integrating telemetry movements.

Another thing to note is that your encounter model needs to be “CLOG” if you have binary observations, to accommodate the RSF integration. But that gets at another strategy you could use, which is to collapse the occasions into categories of max temp (e.g., high, medium, low) and model the captures as Poisson with an offset for number of true occasions in each category. This would be an approximation and maybe would only work if the capture rate were a typical low value.

I do agree with Andy that these model run times are not so bad, especially if you stuck with the current resolution and trimS.

As far as secr goes, my one warning is that many folks have had trouble with telemetry integration and big datasets like yours. So while secr generally is faster, for your particular application it may not be.
